procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and decree dated November 29, 1960 of the Madras High Court in Appeal Suit No. 207 of 1957.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Trial Court upheld the contention of Natarajan Chettiar (respondent No. 3) that properties in schedule D were not liable to be partitioned. The High Court heard the appeal (Appeal Suit No. 207 of 1957) and issued a judgment and decree on November 29, 1960.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants appealed the judgment and decree of the Madras High Court to the Supreme Court after the High Court granted a certificate to do so.

directions: with costs to to the plaintiff-respondent

issue.issue_text: whether the plaintiff-respondent was the son of Rangaswami Chettiar

facts: The trial court and the High Court both found that the plaintiff-respondent was the son of Rangaswami Chettiar, creating a "concurrent finding of fact."
The appellants (the deceased's other wives) argued against this, pointing to a notice where Rangaswami Chettiar had denied paternity.
The plaintiff's mother, Lakshmiammal, testified that she had not left her husband and that the plaintiff was his son. The High Court did not disbelieve her testimony.
Evidence showed that even if Lakshmiammal was living separately, her father's house was only a furlong away from Rangaswami Chettiar's house.
law: The Supreme Court stated that it ordinarily does not interfere with a concurrent finding of fact from lower courts.
The Court relied on Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act, which establishes a "conclusive presumption" that a child born during a valid marriage is the legitimate son of the husband.
To rebut this presumption, the party denying paternity has a "heavy burden" to prove that the husband and wife had "no access to each other at any time when he could have been begotten."
application: The Court reasoned that the notice from Rangaswami Chettiar denying paternity was not strong enough evidence to overcome the conclusive presumption of Section 112.
The appellants were required to prove that Rangaswami Chettiar had no access to Lakshmiammal during the period of conception.
The Court found that the evidence, particularly the fact that the couple lived only a furlong apart, fell "far short" of proving non-access.
The Court accepted the mother's testimony, which had not been disbelieved by the High Court, as further support.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellants had completely failed to prove non-access and therefore could not rebut the strong legal presumption of legitimacy. Consequently, the Court upheld the findings of the lower courts and held that the plaintiff-respondent was the legitimate son of Rangaswami Chettiar.

issue.issue_text: whether the deed of gift was valid

facts: A husband, R, executed a deed of gift for some ancestral immovable property in favor of his second wife.

The wife (the donee-appellant) argued that the gift was valid because it was a reasonable portion of the property, made out of love and affection, and was intended to fulfill a pious obligation to carry out the wishes of her husband's father.
law: Under Hindu law, a father or managing member of a family can make a gift of a reasonable portion of ancestral immovable property for "pious purposes."
A gift of ancestral property to a daughter at the time of her marriage is considered a pious purpose.

There is no authority or precedent in Hindu law to support the proposition that a husband can gift ancestral immovable property to his wife, or that a father-in-law can gift it to his daughter-in-law.
A gift from a husband to a wife out of love and affection is not permitted under Hindu law if the property is ancestral and immovable.
application: The Court refused to extend the scope of "pious purposes" to include a gift from a husband to his wife.

The Court distinguished this case from a gift to a daughter, reasoning that a daughter-in-law becomes a member of the new family and acquires rights to the property, unlike a daughter who is leaving her father's family.

The Court rejected the argument that the husband was fulfilling a pious obligation from his father, stating that even the father-in-law himself would not have been competent to make such a gift of ancestral immovable property.
The Court found no legal basis to uphold a gift of ancestral immovable property from a husband to his wife made simply out of affection.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the deed of gift was not valid because a gift of ancestral immovable property from a husband to his wife is not permitted under Hindu law, as it does not qualify as a "pious purpose."

issue.issue_text: whether a gift of ancestral immovable property made out of affection by a husband to his wife is permitted under Hindu Law

facts: A husband made a gift of ancestral immovable property to his wife.
The gift was made out of love and affection.
The wife (the donee-appellant) argued that the gift was valid.
law: Under Hindu Law, the power to gift ancestral immovable property is highly restricted.
A Hindu father or managing member of a family can only make a gift of ancestral immovable property for 'pious purposes' and the gift must be within reasonable limits.
While gifts of ancestral movable property can be made out of affection to a wife or daughter within reasonable limits, this rule does not extend to immovable property.
A gift of a reasonable portion of ancestral immovable property to a daughter at the time of her marriage is considered a 'pious purpose' because it fulfills a moral obligation.
application: The Court examined whether a gift of ancestral immovable property from a husband to his wife out of affection could be considered a 'pious purpose'.
It found no precedent or authority in Hindu Law that permits such a gift.
The Court explicitly refused to extend the scope of 'pious purposes' to include gifts made by a husband to his wife out of affection.

It distinguished this situation from a gift to a daughter upon her marriage. A gift to a daughter is permissible as she is leaving the family and it is a moral obligation of the father to provide for her. In contrast, a wife becomes a member of the husband's family and is not in the same position.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the validity of the gift, concluding that under Hindu Law, a husband is not permitted to make a gift of ancestral immovable property to his wife out of affection, as this does not qualify as a 'pious purpose'.

issue.issue_text: whether a father-in-law can make a gift of ancestral immovable property in favour of his daughter-in-law at the time of her marriage

law.description: Under Hindu law, a father or managing member of a family can only make a gift of ancestral immovable property within reasonable limits and for "pious purposes".

A gift of ancestral immovable property by a father to his own daughter at the time of her marriage is considered a "pious purpose" because it is the father's duty to marry her and she is leaving the family.

Gifts made by a father-in-law to his daughter-in-law in token of love are permitted and become her 'stridhan' (separate property), but this rule generally applies to movable property or non-ancestral immovable property.

application.description: The Court distinguished the position of a daughter-in-law from that of a daughter. Unlike a daughter who leaves the family upon marriage, a daughter-in-law becomes a member of her father-in-law's family.

As a member of the new family, the daughter-in-law would be entitled to the ancestral property in her own right under certain circumstances. Therefore, a gift to her does not serve the same "pious purpose" as a gift to a departing daughter.

The Court reconciled the 'stridhan' rule with the ancestral property rule by stating that they must be read harmoniously. If a father-in-law cannot gift ancestral immovable property, he cannot do so under the guise of it becoming 'stridhan'. Any gift of immovable property that becomes 'stridhan' must be of property that is not ancestral.
The Court found no authority or precedent in Hindu law to support the proposition that a father-in-law can gift ancestral immovable property to his daughter-in-law.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a father-in-law cannot make a gift of ancestral immovable property to his daughter-in-law at the time of her marriage. The Court reasoned that such a gift does not qualify as a "pious purpose" under Hindu law, unlike a gift to one's own daughter, because the daughter-in-law becomes a member of the family and acquires rights to the property in her own capacity.

arguments.issue_text: whether the plaintiff-respondent was the son of Rangaswami Chettiar
appellant_arguments: The plaintiff, though born to Lakshmiammal, was not the son of Rangaswami Chettiar and was therefore not entitled to any share in his properties.
respondent_arguments: The plaintiff was the son of Rangaswami Chettiar and was entitled to a half share in the joint family properties.

arguments.issue_text: whether the deed of gift was valid
appellant_arguments: The gift deed in favour of Ammathayee (the donee-appellant) was valid.
respondent_arguments: The gift deed was not valid as it was a gift of joint family property.

arguments.issue_text: whether a gift of ancestral immovable property made out of affection by a husband to his wife is permitted under Hindu Law
appellant_arguments: The gift was valid as it was of a reasonable portion of the immovable property and was made by a husband in favour of his wife out of love and affection.
respondent_arguments: A gift of ancestral immovable property by a husband to his wife out of affection is not permitted under Hindu Law.

arguments.issue_text: whether a father-in-law can make a gift of ancestral immovable property in favour of his daughter-in-law at the time of her marriage
appellant_arguments: The gift made by the husband was valid because it was made to carry out the pious obligation to fulfill the wishes of his father (the father-in-law) to make some provision for the daughter-in-law, which the father had indicated at the time of her marriage.
respondent_arguments: A gift of ancestral immovable property by a father-in-law to a daughter-in-law is not permitted, and there is no pious obligation on a son to make such a gift on his father's behalf.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under Hindu Law, a gift of ancestral immovable property by a husband to his wife out of love and affection is not permitted, as it does not constitute a 'pious purpose'. A father-in-law cannot make a gift of ancestral immovable property to a daughter-in-law, and therefore, a son is not under a pious obligation to make such a gift to fulfill his father's wishes.
obiter: A gift of ancestral immovable property by a father to a daughter at the time of her marriage may be considered a pious purpose.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A gift of ancestral immovable property by a husband to his wife out of affection is not permitted under Hindu Law, as it does not fall within the scope of "pious purposes." Similarly, a father-in-law is not competent to make a gift of ancestral immovable property to his daughter-in-law at the time of her marriage, and therefore, a son has no pious obligation to make such a gift on his father's behalf, as this would permit indirectly what is not permitted directly.
legal_tests_applied: Whether a gift of ancestral immovable property falls within the established meaning of "pious purposes" under Hindu Law. The scope of "pious purposes" has been extended by courts to include reasonable gifts to a daughter at the time of her marriage, but the court tests whether any further extension is warranted.
why_appellant_lost: The court found no precedent or authority in Hindu Law to uphold a gift of immovable ancestral property made by a husband to his wife out of affection and saw no reason to extend the scope of "pious purposes" to include such a gift.
The court held that a father-in-law is not competent to make a gift of ancestral immovable property to his daughter-in-law at the time of her marriage, as it cannot be considered a "pious purpose."

The court reasoned that an act which the father-in-law himself could not legally perform cannot be transformed into a "pious obligation" for the son. Allowing the son to make the gift on his father's behalf would be "permitting indirectly what is not permitted under Hindu law directly."
why_respondent_won: The respondent's argument that a gift of ancestral immovable property by a husband to his wife out of affection is not permitted under Hindu Law was accepted by the court.

The respondent's contention that a father-in-law cannot make such a gift and that there is no pious obligation on a son to do so was upheld, as the court found no authority to support such a proposition and concluded it was not a pious purpose.
policy_considerations: The court distinguished the case of a daughter from that of a daughter-in-law. A gift to a daughter is permissible as a pious purpose because she is leaving her father's family, and it is the father's duty to provide for her at marriage.

A gift to a daughter-in-law is not a pious purpose because, upon marriage, she becomes a member of her father-in-law's family and would be entitled to the ancestral property in her own right in certain circumstances, placing her on a "very different footing" from a daughter.
